### Launch preparation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Launch preparation")]

See also: [Launch commit criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_commit_criteria "Launch commit criteria")

[![Image 21: The Space Shuttle moving to the launch complex on a crawler-transporter](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Crawler_transporter_with_Atlantis_on_the_ramp_to_pad_39A.jpg/250px-Crawler_transporter_with_Atlantis_on_the_ramp_to_pad_39A.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crawler_transporter_with_Atlantis_on_the_ramp_to_pad_39A.jpg)

The crawler-transporter with _Atlantis_ on the ramp to LC-39A for [STS-117](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-117 "STS-117")

The Space Shuttle was prepared for launch primarily in the VAB at the KSC. The SRBs were assembled and attached to the external tank on the MLP. The orbiter vehicle was prepared at the [Orbiter Processing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Processing_Facility "Orbiter Processing Facility") (OPF) and transferred to the VAB, where a crane was used to rotate it to the vertical orientation and mate it to the external tank.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):132–133 Once the entire stack was assembled, the MLP was carried for 5.6 km (3.5 mi) to [Launch Complex 39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_Complex_39 "Launch Complex 39") by one of the [crawler-transporters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawler-transporter "Crawler-transporter").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):137 After the Space Shuttle arrived at one of the two launchpads, it would connect to the Fixed and Rotation Service Structures, which provided servicing capabilities, payload insertion, and crew transportation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):139–141 The crew was transported to the launch pad at T−3 hours and entered the orbiter vehicle, which was closed at T−2 hours.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III–8 Liquid oxygen and hydrogen were loaded into the external tank via umbilicals that attached to the orbiter vehicle, which began at T−5 hours 35 minutes. At T−3 hours 45 minutes, the hydrogen fast-fill was complete, followed 15 minutes later by the oxygen tank fill. Both tanks were slowly filled up until the launch as the oxygen and hydrogen evaporated.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II–186

The [launch commit criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_commit_criteria "Launch commit criteria") considered precipitation, temperatures, cloud cover, lightning forecast, wind, and humidity.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-weather_launch_criteria-41) The Space Shuttle was not launched under conditions where it could have been struck by [lightning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning "Lightning"), as its exhaust plume could have triggered lightning by providing a current path to ground after launch, which occurred on [Apollo 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_12#Mission_highlights "Apollo 12").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-chaikin-42):239 The NASA Anvil Rule for a Shuttle launch stated that an [anvil cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anvil_cloud "Anvil cloud") could not appear within a distance of 19[km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre "Kilometre") (10 nmi).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-anvil-43) The Shuttle Launch Weather Officer monitored conditions until the final decision to scrub a launch was announced. In addition to the weather at the launch site, conditions had to be acceptable at one of the [Transatlantic Abort Landing sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_abort_modes#Transoceanic_abort_landing "Space Shuttle abort modes") and the SRB recovery area.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-weather_launch_criteria-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-sts121_blog-44)

Two built-in holds at T−20 minutes and T−9 minutes provided scheduled breaks to address any issues and additional preparation.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III–8 After the built-in hold at T−9 minutes, the countdown was automatically controlled by the Ground Launch Sequencer (GLS) at the LCC, which stopped the countdown if it sensed a critical problem with any of the Space Shuttle's onboard systems.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-sts121_blog-44) At T−3 minutes 45 seconds, the engines began conducting gimbal tests, which were concluded at T−2 minutes 15 seconds. The ground [Launch Processing System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_Processing_System "Launch Processing System") handed off the control to the orbiter vehicle's GPCs at T−31 seconds. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Partially reusable launch system and space plane

This article is about the complete Space Shuttle system (booster, external tank, orbiter) used by NASA. For space shuttles in general, see [Spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft") and [Spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane"). For the spaceplane component of the Space Shuttle, see [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter").

The **Space Shuttle** is a retired, partially [reusable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reusable_launch_system "Reusable launch system")[low Earth orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit")[spacecraft system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NASA_launch_vehicles "List of NASA launch vehicles") operated from 1981 to 2011 by the U.S. [National Aeronautics and Space Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aeronautics_and_Space_Administration "National Aeronautics and Space Administration") (NASA) as part of the [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"). Its official program name was the [Space Transportation System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System "Space Transportation System") (STS), taken from the 1969 plan led by U.S. vice president [Spiro Agnew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiro_Agnew "Spiro Agnew") for a system of reusable spacecraft where it was the only item funded for development.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):163–166[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-space_task_group_1969-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-11)

The first ([STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")) of four orbital test flights occurred in 1981, leading to operational flights ([STS-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-5 "STS-5")) beginning in 1982. Five complete Space Shuttle orbiter vehicles were built and flown on a total of 135 missions from 1981 to 2011. They launched from the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC) in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). Operational missions launched numerous [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite"), [interplanetary probes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interplanetary_probe "Interplanetary probe"), and the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") (HST), conducted science experiments in orbit, participated in the [Shuttle-_Mir_ program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle%E2%80%93Mir_program "Shuttle–Mir program") with Russia, and participated in the construction and servicing of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS). The Space Shuttle fleet's total mission time was 1,323 days.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-ShuttleByNumbers-12)

Space Shuttle components include the [Orbiter Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") (OV) with three clustered [Rocketdyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocketdyne "Rocketdyne")[RS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RS-25 "RS-25") main engines, a pair of recoverable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster") (SRBs), and the expendable [external tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank "Space Shuttle external tank") (ET) containing [liquid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_hydrogen "Liquid hydrogen") and [liquid oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen "Liquid oxygen"). The Space Shuttle was [launched vertically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takeoff_and_landing "Takeoff and landing"), like a conventional rocket, with the two SRBs operating in parallel with the orbiter's three RS-25 main engines, which were fueled from the ET. The SRBs were jettisoned before the vehicle reached orbit, while the main engines continued to operate, and the ET was jettisoned after main engine cutoff and just before [orbit insertion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_insertion "Orbit insertion"), which used the orbiter's two [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS) engines. At the conclusion of the mission, the orbiter fired its OMS to deorbit and [reenter the atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_reentry "Atmospheric reentry"). The orbiter was protected during reentry by its [thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_protection_system "Thermal protection system") tiles, and it [glided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_glider "Rocket glider") as a [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") to a runway landing, usually to the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at KSC, Florida, or to [Rogers Dry Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers_Dry_Lake "Rogers Dry Lake") in [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), California. If the landing occurred at Edwards, the orbiter was flown back to the KSC atop the [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") (SCA), a specially modified [Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") designed to carry the shuttle above it.

The first orbiter, _[Enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise")_, was built in 1976 and used in [Approach and Landing Tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") (ALT), but had no orbital capability. Four fully operational orbiters were initially built: _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_, _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_, and _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. Of these, two were lost in mission accidents: [_Challenger_ in 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") and [_Columbia_ in 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), with a total of 14 astronauts killed. A fifth operational (and sixth in total) orbiter, _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_, was built in 1991 to replace _Challenger_. The three surviving operational vehicles were retired from service following _Atlantis_'s [final flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135") on July 21, 2011. The U.S. relied on the Russian [Soyuz spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)") to transport astronauts to the ISS from the last Shuttle flight until the launch of the [Crew Dragon Demo-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Dragon_Demo-2 "Crew Dragon Demo-2") mission in May 2020.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-13)

## Design and development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Design and development")]

### Historical background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Historical background")]

In the late 1930s, the German government launched the "[Amerikabomber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amerikabomber "Amerikabomber")" (English: America bomber) project, and [Eugen Sänger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_S%C3%A4nger "Eugen Sänger")'s idea, together with mathematician [Irene Bredt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_S%C3%A4nger-Bredt "Irene Sänger-Bredt"), was a winged rocket called the [Silbervogel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silbervogel "Silbervogel") (German for "silver bird").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-14) During the 1950s, the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") proposed using a reusable piloted glider to perform military operations such as reconnaissance, satellite attack, and air-to-ground weapons employment. In the late 1950s, the Air Force began developing the partially reusable [X-20 Dyna-Soar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_X-20_Dyna-Soar "Boeing X-20 Dyna-Soar"). The Air Force collaborated with [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") on the Dyna-Soar and began training six pilots in June 1961. The rising costs of development and the prioritization of [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini") led to the cancellation of the Dyna-Soar program in December 1963. In addition to the Dyna-Soar, the Air Force had conducted a study in 1957 to test the feasibility of reusable boosters. This became the basis for the [aerospaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospaceplane "Aerospaceplane"), a fully reusable spacecraft that was never developed beyond the initial design phase in 1962–1963.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):162–163

Beginning in the early 1950s, NASA and the Air Force collaborated on developing [lifting bodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifting_bodies "Lifting bodies") to test aircraft that primarily generated lift from their fuselages instead of wings, and tested the [NASA M2-F1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_M2-F1 "NASA M2-F1"), [Northrop M2-F2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_M2-F2 "Northrop M2-F2"), [Northrop M2-F3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_M2-F3 "Northrop M2-F3"), [Northrop HL-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_HL-10 "Northrop HL-10"), [Martin Marietta X-24A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta_X-24 "Martin Marietta X-24"), and the [Martin Marietta X-24B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta_X-24#X-24B_2 "Martin Marietta X-24"). The program tested aerodynamic characteristics that would later be incorporated in design of the Space Shuttle, including unpowered landing from a high altitude and speed.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-lifting_body_report-15):142[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):16–18

### Design process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design process")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle design process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_design_process "Space Shuttle design process")

On September 24, 1966, as the Apollo space program neared its design completion, NASA and the Air Force released a joint study concluding that a new vehicle was required to satisfy their respective future demands and that a partially reusable system would be the most cost-effective solution.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):164 The head of the NASA Office of Manned Space Flight, [George Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mueller_(NASA) "George Mueller (NASA)"), announced the plan for a reusable shuttle on August 10, 1968. NASA issued a [request for proposal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_proposal "Request for proposal") (RFP) for designs of the Integral Launch and Reentry Vehicle (ILRV) on October 30, 1968.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-17) Rather than award a contract based upon initial proposals, NASA announced a phased approach for the Space Shuttle contracting and development; Phase A was a request for studies completed by competing aerospace companies, Phase B was a competition between two contractors for a specific contract, Phase C involved designing the details of the spacecraft components, and Phase D was the production of the spacecraft.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-lindroos-18)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):19–22

In December 1968, NASA created the Space Shuttle Task Group to determine the optimal design for a reusable spacecraft, and issued study contracts to [General Dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dynamics "General Dynamics"), [Lockheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Corporation "Lockheed Corporation"), [McDonnell Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas "McDonnell Douglas"), and [North American Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Rockwell "North American Rockwell"). In July 1969, the Space Shuttle Task Group issued a report that determined the Shuttle would support short-duration crewed missions and a space station, as well as the capabilities to launch, service, and retrieve satellites. The report also created three classes of a future reusable shuttle: Class I would have a reusable orbiter mounted on expendable boosters, Class II would use multiple expendable rocket engines and a single propellant tank (stage-and-a-half), and Class III would have both a reusable orbiter and a reusable booster. In September 1969, the Space Task Group, under the leadership of U.S. vice president [Spiro Agnew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiro_Agnew "Spiro Agnew"), issued a report calling for the development of a space shuttle to bring people and cargo to low Earth orbit (LEO), as well as a [space tug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tug "Space tug") for transfers between orbits and the Moon, and a reusable [nuclear upper stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_propulsion#Spacecraft "Nuclear propulsion") for deep space travel.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):163–166[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-space_task_group_1969-10)

After the release of the Space Shuttle Task Group report, many aerospace engineers favored the Class III, fully reusable design because of perceived savings in hardware costs. [Max Faget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Faget "Max Faget"), a NASA engineer who had worked to design the [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") capsule, patented a design for a two-stage fully recoverable system with a straight-winged orbiter mounted on a larger straight-winged booster.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-faget_bio-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-faget_patent-20) The Air Force Flight Dynamics Laboratory argued that a straight-wing design would not be able to withstand the high thermal and aerodynamic stresses during reentry, and would not provide the required cross-range capability. Additionally, the Air Force required a larger payload capacity than Faget's design allowed. In January 1971, NASA and Air Force leadership decided that a reusable delta-wing orbiter mounted on an expendable propellant tank would be the optimal design for the Space Shuttle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):166

After they established the need for a reusable, heavy-lift spacecraft, NASA and the Air Force determined the design requirements of their respective services. The Air Force expected to use the Space Shuttle to launch large satellites, and required it to be capable of lifting 29,000 kg (65,000 lb) to an eastward LEO or 18,000 kg (40,000 lb) into a [polar orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_orbit "Polar orbit"). The satellite designs also required that the Space Shuttle have a 4.6 by 18 m (15 by 60 ft) payload bay. NASA evaluated the [F-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocketdyne_F-1 "Rocketdyne F-1") and [J-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocketdyne_J-2 "Rocketdyne J-2") engines from the [Saturn rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_(rocket_family) "Saturn (rocket family)"), and determined that they were insufficient for the requirements of the Space Shuttle; in July 1971, it issued a contract to [Rocketdyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocketdyne "Rocketdyne") to begin development on the [RS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RS-25 "RS-25") engine.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):165–170

NASA reviewed 29 potential designs for the Space Shuttle and determined that a design with two side boosters should be used, and the boosters should be reusable to reduce costs.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):167 NASA and the Air Force elected to use [solid-propellant boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-propellant_rocket "Solid-propellant rocket") because of the lower costs and the ease of refurbishing them for reuse after they landed in the ocean. In January 1972, President [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon") approved the Shuttle, and NASA decided on its final design in March. The development of the Space Shuttle Main Engine (SSME) remained the responsibility of Rocketdyne, and the contract was issued in July 1971, and updated SSME specifications were submitted to Rocketdyne that April.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-21) The following August, NASA awarded the contract to build the orbiter to North American Rockwell, which had by then constructed a full-scale mock-up, later named _[Inspiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Inspiration "Space Shuttle Inspiration")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-Campa_2024-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-Lost_LA_S7E1-23) In August 1973, NASA awarded the external tank contract to [Martin Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta"), and in November the solid-rocket booster contract to [Morton Thiokol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Thiokol "Morton Thiokol").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):170–173

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 8: The Space Shuttle Columbia under construction](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/566175main_columbia-opf.jpg/250px-566175main_columbia-opf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:566175main_columbia-opf.jpg)

[_Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") undergoing installation of its ceramic tiles

On June 4, 1974, Rockwell began construction on the first orbiter, OV-101, dubbed Constitution, later to be renamed [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"). _Enterprise_ was designed as a test vehicle, and did not include engines or heat shielding. Construction was completed on September 17, 1976, and _Enterprise_ was moved to the [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") to begin testing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):173[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-enterprise_overview-24) Rockwell constructed the [Main Propulsion Test Article (MPTA)-098](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MPTA-098 "MPTA-098"), which was a structural truss mounted to the ET with three RS-25 engines attached. It was tested at the [National Space Technology Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stennis_Space_Center "Stennis Space Center") (NSTL) to ensure that the engines could safely run through the launch profile.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-163 Rockwell conducted mechanical and thermal stress tests on Structural Test Article (STA)-099 to determine the effects of aerodynamic and thermal stresses during launch and reentry.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):I-415

The beginning of the development of the RS-25 Space Shuttle Main Engine was delayed for nine months while [Pratt & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney "Pratt & Whitney") challenged the contract that had been issued to Rocketdyne. The first engine was completed in March 1975, after issues with developing the first throttleable, reusable engine. During engine testing, the RS-25 experienced multiple nozzle failures, as well as broken turbine blades. Despite the problems during testing, NASA ordered the nine RS-25 engines needed for its three orbiters under construction in May 1978.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):174–175

NASA experienced significant delays in the development of the Space Shuttle's [thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"). Previous NASA spacecraft had used [ablative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_entry#Ablative "Atmospheric entry") heat shields, but those could not be reused. NASA chose to use ceramic tiles for thermal protection, as the shuttle could then be constructed of lightweight [aluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum "Aluminum"), and the tiles could be individually replaced as needed. Construction began on [_Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on March 27, 1975, and it was delivered to the KSC on March 25, 1979.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):175–177 At the time of its arrival at the KSC, _Columbia_ still had 6,000 of its 30,000 tiles remaining to be installed. However, many of the tiles that had been originally installed had to be replaced, requiring two years of installation before _Columbia_ could fly.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):46–48

On January 5, 1979, NASA commissioned a second orbiter. Later that month, Rockwell began converting STA-099 to OV-099, later named [_Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger"). On January 29, 1979, NASA ordered two additional orbiters, OV-103 and OV-104, which were named [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") and [_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis"). Construction of OV-105, later named [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour"), began in February 1982, but NASA decided to limit the Space Shuttle fleet to four orbiters in 1983. After the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), NASA resumed production of _Endeavour_ in September 1987.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):52–53

### Testing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Testing")]

[![Image 9: Enterprise being release from the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the Approach and Landing Tests](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/OV-101_first_flight.jpg/250px-OV-101_first_flight.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OV-101_first_flight.jpg)

_Enterprise_ during the [Approach and Landing Tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests")

[![Image 10: The Space Shuttle Columbia launching on the first Space Shuttle mission](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching_cropped_2.jpg/250px-Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching_cropped_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_Columbia_launching_cropped_2.jpg)

[_Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") launching on [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-26)

After it arrived at Edwards AFB, _Enterprise_ underwent flight testing with the [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft"), a Boeing 747 that had been modified to carry the orbiter. In February 1977, _Enterprise_ began the [Approach and Landing Tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") (ALT) and underwent captive flights, where it remained attached to the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the duration of the flight. On August 12, 1977, _Enterprise_ conducted its first glide test, where it detached from the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft and landed at Edwards AFB.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):173–174 After four additional flights, _Enterprise_ was moved to the [Marshall Space Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Space_Flight_Center "Marshall Space Flight Center") (MSFC) on March 13, 1978. _Enterprise_ underwent shake tests in the Mated Vertical Ground Vibration Test, where it was attached to an external tank and solid rocket boosters, and underwent vibrations to simulate the stresses of launch. In April 1979, _Enterprise_ was taken to the KSC, where it was attached to an external tank and solid rocket boosters, and moved to [LC-39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39 "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39"). Once installed at the launch pad, the Space Shuttle was used to verify the proper positioning of the launch complex hardware. _Enterprise_ was taken back to California in August 1979, and later served in the development of the [SLC-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_AFB_Space_Launch_Complex_6 "Vandenberg AFB Space Launch Complex 6") at [Vandenberg AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_AFB "Vandenberg AFB") in 1984.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):40–41

On November 24, 1980, _Columbia_ was mated with its external tank and solid-rocket boosters, and was moved to LC-39 on December 29.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III-22 The first Space Shuttle mission, [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1"), would be the first time NASA performed a crewed first-flight of a spacecraft.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III-24 On April 12, 1981, the Space Shuttle launched for the first time, and was piloted by [John Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Young_(astronaut) "John Young (astronaut)") and [Robert Crippen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Crippen "Robert Crippen"). During the two-day mission, Young and Crippen tested equipment on board the shuttle, and found several of the ceramic tiles had fallen off the top side of the _Columbia_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-into_the_black-27):277–278 NASA coordinated with the Air Force to use satellites to image the underside of _Columbia_, and determined there was no damage.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-into_the_black-27):335–337 _Columbia_ reentered the atmosphere and landed at Edwards AFB on April 14.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III-24

NASA conducted three additional test flights with _Columbia_ in 1981 and 1982. On July 4, 1982, [STS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-4 "STS-4"), flown by [Ken Mattingly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Mattingly "Ken Mattingly") and [Henry Hartsfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hartsfield "Henry Hartsfield"), landed on a concrete runway at Edwards AFB. President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") and his wife [Nancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Reagan "Nancy Reagan") met the crew, and delivered a speech. After STS-4, NASA declared its Space Transportation System (STS) operational.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-dev_space_shuttle-9):178–179[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-28)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Description")]

The Space Shuttle was the first operational orbital spacecraft designed for [reuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reusable_launch_system "Reusable launch system"). Each Space Shuttle orbiter was designed for a projected lifespan of 100 launches or ten years of operational life, although this was later extended.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-sivolella-29):11 At launch, it consisted of the [orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"), which contained the [crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Space_Shuttle_crews "List of Space Shuttle crews") and payload, the [external tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank "Space Shuttle external tank") (ET), and the two [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster") (SRBs).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):363

Responsibility for the Space Shuttle components was spread among multiple NASA field centers. The KSC was responsible for launch, landing, and turnaround operations for equatorial orbits (the only orbit profile actually used in the program). The U.S. Air Force at the [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") was responsible for launch, landing, and turnaround operations for polar orbits (though this was never used). The [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") (JSC) served as the central point for all Shuttle operations and the MSFC was responsible for the main engines, external tank, and solid rocket boosters. The [John C. Stennis Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Stennis_Space_Center "John C. Stennis Space Center") handled main engine testing, and the [Goddard Space Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_Space_Flight_Center "Goddard Space Flight Center") managed the global tracking network.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-30)

### Orbiter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Orbiter")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter")

[![Image 11: The five Space Shuttle orbiters launching](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Shuttle_profiles.jpg/960px-Shuttle_profiles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shuttle_profiles.jpg)

Shuttle launch profiles. From left: _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_, _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_, _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_, and _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_

The orbiter had design elements and capabilities of both a rocket and an aircraft to allow it to launch vertically and then land as a glider.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):365 Its three-part fuselage provided support for the crew compartment, cargo bay, flight surfaces, and engines. The rear of the orbiter contained the Space Shuttle Main Engines (SSME), which provided thrust during launch, as well as the Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS), which allowed the orbiter to achieve, alter, and exit its orbit once in space. Its cropped-compound [delta wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_wing "Delta wing") were 18 m (60 ft) long, and were swept 81° at the inner leading edge and 45° at the outer leading edge. Each wing had an inboard and outboard [elevon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevon "Elevon") to provide flight control during reentry, along with a flap located between the wings, below the engines to control [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_principal_axes#Transverse_axis_(pitch) "Aircraft principal axes"). The orbiter's [vertical stabilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_stabilizer "Vertical stabilizer") was swept backwards at 45° and contained a [rudder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder#Aircraft_rudders "Rudder") that could split to act as a [speed brake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_brake_(aeronautics) "Air brake (aeronautics)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):382–389 The vertical stabilizer also contained a two-part [drag parachute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drogue_parachute "Drogue parachute") system to slow the orbiter after landing. The orbiter used [retractable landing gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_gear#Retractable_gear "Landing gear") with a nose landing gear and two main landing gear, each containing two tires. The main landing gear contained two brake assemblies each, and the nose landing gear contained an electro-hydraulic steering mechanism.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):408–411

#### Crew

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Crew")]

The Space Shuttle crew varied per mission. They underwent rigorous testing and training to meet the [qualification requirements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut#NASA_candidacy_requirements "Astronaut") for their roles. The crew was divided into three categories: Pilots, Mission Specialists, and Payload Specialists. Pilots were further divided into two roles: the Space Shuttle Commander sat in the forward left seat, and the Space Shuttle Pilot sat in the forward right seat.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-31) The test flights, STS-1 through STS-4 only had two members each, the commander and pilot. The commander and the pilot were both qualified to fly and land the orbiter. The on-orbit operations, such as experiments, payload deployment, and EVAs, were conducted primarily by the mission specialists who were specifically trained for their intended missions and systems. Early in the Space Shuttle program, NASA flew with payload specialists, who were typically systems specialists who worked for the company paying for the payload's deployment or operations. The final payload specialist, [Gregory B. Jarvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_B._Jarvis "Gregory B. Jarvis"), flew on [STS-51-L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-L "STS-51-L"), and future non-pilots were designated as mission specialists. An astronaut flew as a crewed spaceflight engineer on both [STS-51-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-C "STS-51-C") and [STS-51-J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-J "STS-51-J") to serve as a military representative for a [National Reconnaissance Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Reconnaissance_Office "National Reconnaissance Office") payload. A Space Shuttle crew typically had seven astronauts, with [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A") flying with eight.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III-21

#### Crew compartment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Crew compartment")]

The crew compartment comprised three decks and was the pressurized, habitable area on all Space Shuttle missions. The flight deck consisted of two seats for the commander and pilot, as well as an additional two to four seats for crew members. The mid-deck was located below the flight deck and was where the galley and crew bunks were set up, as well as three or four crew member seats. The mid-deck contained the airlock, which could support two astronauts on an [extravehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") (EVA), as well as access to pressurized research modules. An equipment bay was below the mid-deck, which stored environmental control and waste management systems.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):60–62[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):365–369

On the first four Shuttle missions, astronauts wore modified U.S. Air Force high-altitude full-pressure suits, which included a full-pressure helmet during ascent and descent. From the fifth flight, [STS-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-5 "STS-5"), until the loss of _Challenger_, the crew wore one-piece light blue [nomex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomex "Nomex") flight suits and partial-pressure helmets. After the _Challenger_ disaster, the crew members wore the Launch Entry Suit (LES), a partial-pressure version of the high-altitude pressure suits with a helmet. In 1994, the LES was replaced by the full-pressure [Advanced Crew Escape Suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Crew_Escape_Suit "Advanced Crew Escape Suit") (ACES), which improved the safety of the astronauts in an emergency situation. _Columbia_ originally had modified [SR-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SR-71 "SR-71")[zero-zero ejection seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-zero_ejection_seat "Zero-zero ejection seat") installed for the [ALT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") and first four missions, but these were disabled after STS-4 and removed after [STS-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-9 "STS-9").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):370–371

[![Image 12: The view from the Atlantis cockpit while in orbit](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/STSCPanel.jpg/250px-STSCPanel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STSCPanel.jpg)

_[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ was the first Shuttle to fly with a [glass cockpit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_cockpit "Glass cockpit"), on [STS-101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-101 "STS-101").

The flight deck was the top level of the crew compartment and contained the flight controls for the orbiter. The commander sat in the front left seat, and the pilot sat in the front right seat, with two to four additional seats set up for additional crew members. The instrument panels contained over 2,100 displays and controls, and the commander and pilot were both equipped with a [heads-up display](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads-up_display "Heads-up display") (HUD) and a [Rotational Hand Controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joystick#Electronic_joysticks "Joystick") (RHC) to [gimbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimbal "Gimbal") the engines during powered flight and fly the orbiter during unpowered flight. Both seats also had [rudder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder "Rudder") controls, to allow rudder movement in flight and nose-wheel steering on the ground.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):369–372 The orbiter vehicles were originally installed with the Multifunction [CRT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode-ray_tube "Cathode-ray tube") Display System (MCDS) to display and control flight information. The MCDS displayed the flight information at the commander and pilot seats, as well as at the aft seating location, and also controlled the data on the HUD. In 1998, _Atlantis_ was upgraded with the Multifunction Electronic Display System (MEDS), which was a [glass cockpit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_cockpit "Glass cockpit") upgrade to the flight instruments that replaced the eight MCDS display units with 11 multifunction colored digital screens. MEDS was flown for the first time in May 2000 on [STS-101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-101 "STS-101"), and the other orbiter vehicles were upgraded to it. The aft section of the flight deck contained windows looking into the payload bay, as well as an RHC to control the [Remote Manipulator System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_Manipulator_System "Remote Manipulator System") during cargo operations. Additionally, the aft flight deck had monitors for a [closed-circuit television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-circuit_television "Closed-circuit television") to view the cargo bay.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):372–376

The mid-deck contained the crew equipment storage, sleeping area, galley, medical equipment, and hygiene stations for the crew. The crew used modular lockers to store equipment that could be scaled depending on their needs, as well as permanently installed floor compartments. The mid-deck contained a port-side hatch that the crew used for entry and exit while on Earth.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II–26–33

#### Airlock

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Airlock")]

The [airlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airlock "Airlock") is a structure installed to allow movement between two spaces with different gas components, conditions, or pressures. Continuing on the mid-deck structure, each orbiter was originally installed with an internal airlock in the mid-deck. The internal airlock was installed as an external airlock in the payload bay on _Discovery_, _Atlantis_, and _Endeavour_ to improve docking with [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") and the [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS "ISS"), along with the [Orbiter Docking System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Docking_System "Orbiter Docking System").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II–26–33 The airlock module can be fitted in the mid-bay, or connected to it but in the payload bay.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):81 With an internal cylindrical volume of 1.60 metres (5 feet 3 inches) diameter and 2.11 metres (6 feet 11 inches) in length, it can hold two suited astronauts. It has two D-shaped hatchways 1.02 m (40 in) long (diameter), and 0.91 m (36 in) wide.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):82

#### Flight systems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Flight systems")]

The orbiter was equipped with an [avionics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avionics "Avionics") system to provide information and control during atmospheric flight. Its avionics suite contained three [microwave scanning beam landing systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave_scanning_beam_landing_system "Microwave scanning beam landing system"), three [gyroscopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyroscope "Gyroscope"), three [TACANs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_air_navigation_system "Tactical air navigation system"), three [accelerometers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerometer "Accelerometer"), two [radar altimeters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar_altimeter "Radar altimeter"), two [barometric altimeters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barometric_altimeter "Barometric altimeter"), three [attitude indicators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attitude_indicator "Attitude indicator"), two [Mach indicators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machmeter "Machmeter"), and two [Mode C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_transponder_interrogation_modes "Aviation transponder interrogation modes")[transponders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transponder_(aeronautics) "Transponder (aeronautics)"). During reentry, the crew deployed two [air data probes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_data_boom "Air data boom") once they were traveling slower than Mach 5. The orbiter had three [inertial measuring units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_measurement_unit "Inertial measurement unit") (IMU) that it used for guidance and navigation during all phases of flight. The orbiter contains two [star trackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_tracker "Star tracker") to align the IMUs while in orbit. The star trackers are deployed while in orbit, and can automatically or manually align on a star. In 1991, NASA began upgrading the inertial measurement units with an [inertial navigation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_navigation_system "Inertial navigation system") (INS), which provided more accurate location information. In 1993, NASA flew a [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPS "GPS") receiver for the first time aboard [STS-51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51 "STS-51"). In 1997, Honeywell began developing an integrated GPS/INS to replace the IMU, INS, and TACAN systems, which first flew on [STS-118](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-118 "STS-118") in August 2007.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):402–403

While in orbit, the crew primarily communicated using one of four [S band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S_band "S band") radios, which provided both voice and data communications. Two of the S band radios were [phase modulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_modulation "Phase modulation")[transceivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transceiver "Transceiver"), and could transmit and receive information. The other two S band radios were [frequency modulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency_modulation "Frequency modulation")[transmitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmitter "Transmitter") and were used to transmit data to NASA. As S band radios can operate only within their [line of sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line-of-sight_propagation "Line-of-sight propagation"), NASA used the [Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") and the [Spacecraft Tracking and Data Acquisition Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_Tracking_and_Data_Acquisition_Network "Spacecraft Tracking and Data Acquisition Network") ground stations to communicate with the orbiter throughout its orbit. Additionally, the orbiter deployed a high-bandwidth [K u band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band "Ku band") radio out of the cargo bay, which could also be utilized as a rendezvous radar. The orbiter was also equipped with two [UHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UHF "UHF") radios for communications with [air traffic control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_control "Air traffic control") and astronauts conducting EVA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):403–404

[![Image 13: The two general-purpose computers used in the orbiter](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Space_Shuttle_General_Purpose_Computer.jpg/250px-Space_Shuttle_General_Purpose_Computer.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Space_Shuttle_General_Purpose_Computer.jpg)

General Purpose Computers: AP-101S (left) and AP-101B CPU with I/O Processor (right)

The Space Shuttle's [fly-by-wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly-by-wire "Fly-by-wire") control system was entirely reliant on its main computer, the Data Processing System (DPS). The DPS controlled the flight controls and thrusters on the orbiter, as well as the ET and SRBs during launch. The DPS consisted of five general-purpose computers (GPC), two magnetic tape mass memory units (MMUs), and the associated sensors to monitor the Space Shuttle components.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):232–233 The original GPC consisted of an IBM [AP-101B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_System/4_Pi#AP-101 "IBM System/4 Pi")[central processing unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPU) and a separate input/output processor (IOP); both contained [non-volatile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-volatile_memory "Non-volatile memory") core memory. From 1991 to 1993, the orbiter vehicles were upgraded to the AP-101S, which improved the memory and processing capabilities, and reduced the volume and weight of the computers by combining the CPU and IOP into a single unit. Four of the GPCs were loaded with the Primary Avionics Software System (PASS), which was Space Shuttle-specific software that provided control through all phases of flight. During ascent, maneuvering, reentry, and landing, the four PASS GPCs functioned identically to produce quadruple redundancy and would error check their results. In case of a software error that would cause erroneous reports from the four PASS GPCs, a fifth GPC ran the Backup Flight System, which used a different program and could control the Space Shuttle through ascent, orbit, and reentry, but could not support an entire mission. The five GPCs were separated in three separate bays within the mid-deck to provide redundancy in the event of a cooling fan failure. The redundancy management system that monitored and managed these redundant components was developed at NASA's Johnson Space Center in the early 1970s.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-32) After achieving orbit, the crew would switch some of the GPCs functions from guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) to systems management (SM) and payload (PL) to support the operational mission.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):405–408 The Space Shuttle was not launched if its flight would run from December to January, as its flight software would have required the orbiter vehicle's computers to be reset at the year change. In 2007, NASA engineers devised a solution so Space Shuttle flights could cross the year-end boundary.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-YERO-33)

Space Shuttle missions typically brought a portable general support computer (PGSC) that could integrate with the orbiter vehicle's computers and communication suite, as well as monitor scientific and payload data. Early missions brought the [Grid Compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_Compass "Grid Compass"), one of the first laptop computers, as the PGSC, but later missions brought [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") and [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") laptops.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):408[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-GRiD-34)

#### Payload bay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Payload bay")]

[![Image 14: An astronaut conducting an EVA while the Hubble Space Telescope is in the payload bay](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Hubble_First_Servicing_EVA_-_GPN-2000-001085.jpg/250px-Hubble_First_Servicing_EVA_-_GPN-2000-001085.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hubble_First_Servicing_EVA_-_GPN-2000-001085.jpg)

[Story Musgrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Story_Musgrave "Story Musgrave") attached to the RMS servicing the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") during [STS-61](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61 "STS-61")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/STS132_Atlantis_undocking2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-STS132_Atlantis_undocking2_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS132_Atlantis_undocking2_(cropped).jpg)

_[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ in orbit in 2010. Image shows the payload bay and the extended [Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm").

The payload bay comprised most of the orbiter vehicle's [fuselage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuselage "Fuselage"), and provided the cargo-carrying space for the Space Shuttle's payloads. It was 18 m (60 ft) long and 4.6 m (15 ft) wide, and could accommodate cylindrical payloads up to 4.6 m (15 ft) in diameter. Two payload bay doors hinged on either side of the bay, and provided a relatively airtight seal to protect payloads from heating during launch and reentry. Payloads were secured in the payload bay to the attachment points on the [longerons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longeron "Longeron"). The payload bay doors served an additional function as radiators for the orbiter vehicle's heat, and were opened upon reaching orbit for heat rejection.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):62–64

The orbiter could be used in conjunction with a variety of add-on components depending on the mission. This included orbital laboratories,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-304,319 boosters for launching payloads farther into space,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-326 the Remote Manipulator System (RMS),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-40 and optionally the EDO pallet to extend the mission duration.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-86 To limit the fuel consumption while the orbiter was docked at the ISS, the [Station-to-Shuttle Power Transfer System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Station-to-Shuttle_Power_Transfer_System "Station-to-Shuttle Power Transfer System") (SSPTS) was developed to convert and transfer station power to the orbiter.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-87–88 The SSPTS was first used on STS-118, and was installed on _Discovery_ and _Endeavour_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):III-366–368

#### Remote Manipulator System

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Remote Manipulator System")]

Main article: [Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")

The Remote Manipulator System (RMS), also known as Canadarm, was a mechanical arm attached to the cargo bay. It could be used to grasp and manipulate payloads, as well as serve as a mobile platform for astronauts conducting an EVA. The RMS was built by the Canadian company [Spar Aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spar_Aerospace "Spar Aerospace") and was controlled by an astronaut inside the orbiter's flight deck using their windows and closed-circuit television. The RMS allowed for six degrees of freedom and had six joints located at three points along the arm. The original RMS could deploy or retrieve payloads up to 29,000 kg (65,000 lb), which was later improved to 270,000 kg (586,000 lb).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):384–385

#### Spacelab

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Spacelab")]

Main article: [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab")

[![Image 16: Spacelab in the payload bay while in orbit](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/STS-9_Spacelab_1.jpg/250px-STS-9_Spacelab_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-9_Spacelab_1.jpg)

[Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") in orbit on [STS-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-9 "STS-9")

The Spacelab module was a European-funded pressurized laboratory that was carried within the payload bay and allowed for scientific research while in orbit. The Spacelab module contained two 2.7 m (9 ft) segments that were mounted in the aft end of the payload bay to maintain the center of gravity during flight. Astronauts entered the Spacelab module through a 2.7 or 5.8 m (8.72 or 18.88 ft) tunnel that connected to the airlock. The Spacelab equipment was primarily stored in pallets, which provided storage for both experiments as well as computer and power equipment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):434–435 Spacelab hardware was flown on 28 missions through 1999 and studied subjects including astronomy, microgravity, radar, and life sciences. Spacelab hardware also supported missions such as Hubble Space Telescope (HST) servicing and space station resupply. The Spacelab module was tested on STS-2 and STS-3, and the first full mission was on STS-9.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-NASA28-35)

#### RS-25 engines

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: RS-25 engines")]

Main article: [RS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RS-25 "RS-25")

[![Image 17: The two engine systems at the aft-section of the orbiter](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/STS-133_Rendezvous_Pitch_Maneuver_3.jpg/250px-STS-133_Rendezvous_Pitch_Maneuver_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-133_Rendezvous_Pitch_Maneuver_3.jpg)

[RS-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RS-25 "RS-25") engines with the two [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS) pods during [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133")

Three RS-25 engines, also known as the Space Shuttle Main Engines (SSME), were mounted on the orbiter's aft fuselage in a triangular pattern. The engine nozzles could gimbal ±10.5° in pitch, and ±8.5° in [yaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_principal_axes#Vertical_axis_(yaw) "Aircraft principal axes") during ascent to change the direction of their thrust to steer the Shuttle. The [titanium alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium_alloy "Titanium alloy") reusable engines were independent of the orbiter vehicle and would be removed and replaced in between flights. The RS-25 is a staged-combustion cycle cryogenic engine that used liquid oxygen and hydrogen and had a higher chamber pressure than any previous liquid-fueled rocket. The original main combustion chamber operated at a maximum pressure of 226.5 bar (3,285 psi). The engine nozzle is 287 cm (113 in) tall and has an interior diameter of 229 cm (90.3 in). The nozzle is cooled by 1,080 interior lines carrying liquid hydrogen and is thermally protected by insulative and ablative material.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II–177–183

The RS-25 engines had several improvements to enhance reliability and power. During the development program, Rocketdyne determined that the engine was capable of safe reliable operation at 104% of the originally specified thrust. To keep the engine thrust values consistent with previous documentation and software, NASA kept the originally specified thrust at 100%, but had the RS-25 operate at higher thrust. RS-25 upgrade versions were denoted as Block I and Block II. 109% thrust level was achieved with the Block II engines in 2001, which reduced the chamber pressure to 207.5 bars (3,010 psi), as it had a larger [throat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Laval_nozzle "De Laval nozzle") area. The normal maximum throttle was 104 percent, with 106% or 109% used for mission aborts.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):106–107

#### Orbital Maneuvering System

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Orbital Maneuvering System")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System")

The Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) consisted of two aft-mounted [AJ10-190](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AJ10 "AJ10") engines and the associated propellant tanks. The AJ10 engines used [monomethylhydrazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomethylhydrazine "Monomethylhydrazine") (MMH) oxidized by [dinitrogen tetroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinitrogen_tetroxide "Dinitrogen tetroxide") (N 2 O 4). The pods carried a maximum of 2,140 kg (4,718 lb) of MMH and 3,526 kg (7,773 lb) of N 2 O 4. The OMS engines were used after main engine cut-off (MECO) for orbital insertion. Throughout the flight, they were used for orbit changes, as well as the deorbit burn prior to reentry. Each OMS engine produced 27,080 N (6,087 lbf) of thrust, and the entire system could provide 305 m/s (1,000 ft/s) of [velocity change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta-v "Delta-v").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II–80

#### Thermal protection system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Thermal protection system")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system")

The orbiter was protected from heat during reentry by the thermal protection system (TPS), a [thermal soaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_entry#Thermal_soak "Atmospheric entry") protective layer around the orbiter. In contrast with previous US spacecraft, which had used ablative heat shields, the reusability of the orbiter required a multi-use heat shield.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):72–73 During reentry, the TPS experienced temperatures up to 1,600°C (3,000°F), but had to keep the orbiter vehicle's aluminum skin temperature below 180°C (350°F). The TPS primarily consisted of four types of tiles. The nose cone and leading edges of the wings experienced temperatures above 1,300°C (2,300°F), and were protected by reinforced carbon-carbon tiles (RCC). Thicker RCC tiles were developed and installed in 1998 to prevent damage from [micrometeoroid and orbital debris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_debris "Space debris"), and were further improved after RCC damage caused in the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). Beginning with [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114"), the orbiter vehicles were equipped with the wing leading edge impact detection system to alert the crew to any potential damage.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II–112–113 The entire underside of the orbiter vehicle, as well as the other hottest surfaces, were protected with tiles of high-temperature reusable surface insulation, made of [borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass")-coated [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica") fibers that trapped heat in air pockets and redirected it out. Areas on the upper parts of the orbiter vehicle were coated in tiles of white low-temperature reusable surface insulation with similar composition, which provided protection for temperatures below 650°C (1,200°F). The payload bay doors and parts of the upper wing surfaces were coated in reusable [Nomex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomex "Nomex") felt surface insulation or in [beta cloth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_cloth "Beta cloth"), as the temperature there remained below 370°C (700°F).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):395

### External tank

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: External tank")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle external tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank "Space Shuttle external tank")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/External_Tank.jpg/250px-External_Tank.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:External_Tank.jpg)

The ET from [STS-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-115 "STS-115") after separation from the orbiter. The scorch mark near the front end of the tank is from the SRB separation motors.

The Space Shuttle external tank (ET) carried the propellant for the Space Shuttle Main Engines, and connected the orbiter vehicle with the solid rocket boosters. The ET was 47 m (153.8 ft) tall and 8.4 m (27.6 ft) in diameter, and contained separate tanks for liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen. The liquid oxygen tank was housed in the nose of the ET, and was 15 m (49.3 ft) tall. The liquid hydrogen tank comprised the bulk of the ET, and was 29 m (96.7 ft) tall. The orbiter vehicle was attached to the ET at two umbilical plates, which contained five propellant and two electrical umbilicals, and forward and aft structural attachments. The exterior of the ET was covered in orange spray-on foam to allow it to survive the heat of ascent.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):421–422

The ET provided propellant to the Space Shuttle Main Engines from liftoff until main engine cutoff. The ET separated from the orbiter vehicle 18 seconds after engine cutoff and could be triggered automatically or manually. At the time of separation, the orbiter vehicle retracted its umbilical plates, and the umbilical cords were sealed to prevent excess propellant from venting into the orbiter vehicle. After the bolts attached at the structural attachments were sheared, the ET separated from the orbiter vehicle. At the time of separation, gaseous oxygen was vented from the nose to cause the ET to tumble, ensuring that it would break up upon reentry. The ET was the only major component of the Space Shuttle system that was not reused, and it would travel along a ballistic trajectory into the Indian or Pacific Ocean.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):422

For the first two missions, STS-1 and [STS-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-2 "STS-2"), the ET was covered in 270 kg (595 lb) of white fire-retardant latex paint to provide protection against damage from ultraviolet radiation. Further research determined that the orange foam itself was sufficiently protected, and the ET was no longer covered in latex paint beginning on STS-3.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins2016-25):II-210 A lightweight tank (LWT) was first flown on STS-6, which reduced tank weight by 4,700 kg (10,300 lb). The LWT's weight was reduced by removing components from the hydrogen tank and reducing the thickness of some skin panels.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):422 In 1998, a super lightweight ET (SLWT) first flew on [STS-91](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-91 "STS-91"). The SLWT used the 2195 aluminum-lithium alloy, which was 40% stronger and 10% less dense than its predecessor, 2219 aluminum-lithium alloy. The SLWT weighed 3,400 kg (7,500 lb) less than the LWT, which allowed the Space Shuttle to deliver heavy elements to ISS's high inclination orbit.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):423–424

### Solid Rocket Boosters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Solid Rocket Boosters")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster")

[![Image 19: Two Solid Rocket Boosters that are not attached to an external tank or orbiter](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Two_Space_Shuttle_SRBs_on_the_Crawler_transporter.jpg/250px-Two_Space_Shuttle_SRBs_on_the_Crawler_transporter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Two_Space_Shuttle_SRBs_on_the_Crawler_transporter.jpg)

Two SRBs on the mobile launcher platform prior to mating with the ET and orbiter for [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134")

The Solid Rocket Boosters (SRB) provided 71.4% of the Space Shuttle's thrust during liftoff and ascent, and were the largest [solid-propellant motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-propellant_motor "Solid-propellant motor") ever flown.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-SRB_largest-7) Each SRB was 45 m (149.2 ft) tall and 3.7 m (12.2 ft) wide, weighed 68,000 kg (150,000 lb), and had a steel exterior approximately 13 mm (.5 in) thick. The SRB's subcomponents were the solid-propellant motor, nose cone, and rocket nozzle. The solid-propellant motor comprised the majority of the SRB's structure. Its casing consisted of 11 steel sections which made up its four main segments. The nose cone housed the forward separation motors and the parachute systems that were used during recovery. The rocket nozzles could gimbal up to 8° to allow for in-flight adjustments.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):425–429

The rocket motors were each filled with a total 500,000 kg (1,106,640 lb) of solid rocket propellant ([APCP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_perchlorate_composite_propellant "Ammonium perchlorate composite propellant")+[PBAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybutadiene_acrylonitrile "Polybutadiene acrylonitrile")), and joined in the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) at KSC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):425–426 In addition to providing thrust during the first stage of launch, the SRBs provided structural support for the orbiter vehicle and ET, as they were the only system that was connected to the [mobile launcher platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_launcher_platform "Mobile launcher platform") (MLP).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):427 At the time of launch, the SRBs were armed at T−5 minutes, and could only be electrically ignited once the RS-25 engines had ignited and were without issue.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):428 They each provided 12,500 kN (2,800,000 lbf) of thrust, which was later improved to 13,300 kN (3,000,000 lbf) beginning on [STS-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-8 "STS-8").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):425 After expending their fuel, the SRBs were [jettisoned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jettison_(aviation) "Jettison (aviation)") approximately two minutes after launch at an altitude of approximately 46 km (150,000 ft). Following separation, they deployed drogue and main parachutes, landed in the ocean, and were recovered by the crews aboard the ships [MV _Freedom Star_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Freedom_Star "MV Freedom Star") and [MV _Liberty Star_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Liberty_Star "MV Liberty Star").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):430 Once they were returned to Cape Canaveral, they were cleaned and disassembled. The rocket motor, igniter, and nozzle were then shipped to Thiokol to be refurbished and reused on subsequent flights.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-shuttle_manual-16):124

The SRBs underwent several redesigns throughout the program's lifetime. [STS-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-6 "STS-6") and [STS-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-7 "STS-7") used SRBs 2,300 kg (5,000 lb) lighter due to walls that were 0.10 mm (.004 in) thinner, but were determined to be too thin to fly safely. Subsequent flights until [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") used cases that were 0.076 mm (.003 in) thinner than the standard-weight cases, which reduced 1,800 kg (4,000 lb). After the _Challenger_ disaster as a result of an [O-ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O-ring "O-ring") failing at low temperature, the SRBs were redesigned to provide a constant seal regardless of the ambient temperature.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-jenkins-3):425–426

### Support vehicles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Support vehicles")]

[![Image 20: A recovery boat with a recovered Solid Rocket Booster](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Freedom_Star_SRB_recovery.jpg/250px-Freedom_Star_SRB_recovery.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Freedom_Star_SRB_recovery.jpg)

MV _Freedom Star_ towing a spent SRB (STS-133) to Cape Canaveral Air Force Station

The Space Shuttle's operations were supported by vehicles and infrastructure that facilitated its transportation, construction, and crew access. The [crawler-transporters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawler-transporter "Crawler-transporter") carried the MLP and the Space Shuttle from the VAB to the launch site.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle#cite_note-crawler-36) The [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") (SCA) were two modified [Boeing 747s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") that could carry an orbiter on its back. The original SCA (N905NA) was first flown in 1975, and was used for the [ALT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") and ferrying the orbiter from Edwards AFB to the KSC on all missions prior to 1991.
